name: Tranexamic acid
lead: Tranexamic acid (TXA) is a synthetic derivative of the amino acid lysine that acts as an antifibrinolytic: it reversibly binds lysine-binding sites on plasminogen, reducing conversion to plasmin and so slowing the breakdown of fibrin clots.[1][2] It is used to prevent or treat bleeding in trauma, postpartum haemorrhage, surgery, tooth removal, nosebleeds and heavy menstrual bleeding, and it is on the WHO List of Essential Medicines.[1]

In dermatology it has become a widely discussed option for melasma and other stubborn hyperpigmentation, used orally, topically, by injection or microneedling-assisted delivery.[3][4][5] Oral TXA for melasma is off-label (it is not approved for that indication by the US FDA or India's regulator, according to a 2023 Indian expert consensus), while topical cosmetic products containing TXA are sold in many markets.[6]

Reviews describe promising results in melasma but heterogeneous study designs, small samples, unknown optimal duration and frequent relapse after treatment stops.[3][6] A systematic review of melasma treatments notes that systemic TXA had promising results but was linked to systemic side effects, and that combination therapies generally performed best.[3] The systemic form carries a thrombosis warning on its drug label.

paras: In appearance medicine, TXA is used for melasma and some post-inflammatory or periorbital hyperpigmentation, in oral, topical, intradermal and microneedling-assisted forms, sometimes combined with lasers, peels or other lightening agents.[3][4][7][8]

The core indications are bleeding. Wikipedia reports that TXA lowers the risk of death in trauma patients with significant bleeding, most effectively when given within three hours, reduces postpartum bleeding deaths, and is used for heavy menstrual bleeding and surgical or dental procedures.[1] The US intravenous label lists short-term use in hemophilia patients around tooth extraction.[9] Large randomized trials such as CRASH-2, WOMAN and CRASH-3 established much of this evidence.[10][11][12]

In melasma, a 2022 systematic review found promising results for systemic TXA and observed that high recurrence characterised all treatment groups, with combination therapies giving the best outcomes.[3] A 2023 Indian expert consensus reviewed about 25 studies published between 2012 and 2022 covering more than 2,000 patients, reported generally improved severity scores with oral TXA alone or with topical agents, lasers or light devices, and cautioned that optimal dose and treatment length are unknown, study designs vary and the authors had company support.[6]

Randomized trials have compared 3 percent TXA cream with 4 percent hydroquinone cream in a split-face design for mixed-type melasma in skin of color,[13] oral versus topical TXA,[5] and TXA/niacinamide creams with hydroquinone.[14] A 2023 review of TXA in dermatology and a trial of topical TXA alone or combined with fractional CO2 laser or microneedling are also available.[4][7]

Human melasma studies include a 2024 double-blind split-face randomized trial of 3 percent TXA versus 4 percent hydroquinone cream,[13] a 2025 randomized trial of oral versus topical TXA,[5] a 2025 randomized double-blind trial of niosomal and conventional TXA/niacinamide creams versus hydroquinone,[14] a trial of topical TXA alone or with laser or microneedling,[7] and a 2022 split-face study comparing microneedling-delivered TXA with vitamin C.[15] The 2023 Indian consensus summarises the oral literature.[6] A registered study evaluates TXA for post-inflammatory pigmentation in a suction blister model (n=10).[16]
Outside dermatology, the evidence base is far larger, including trials in trauma, postpartum haemorrhage, traumatic brain injury, cardiac surgery and heavy menstrual bleeding.[10][11][12][17]

The intravenous US label lists nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, allergic dermatitis, giddiness, hypotension and thromboembolic events as the most common reactions, and warns about thrombosis with concomitant factor IX, seizures after inadvertent neuraxial injection, hypersensitivity, visual disturbances and dizziness.[9] Wikipedia lists color-vision changes, seizures, blood clots and allergic reactions as rare effects.[1]

In melasma, the Indian consensus reports mostly mild effects such as gastrointestinal upset and lighter menstrual flow, one deep vein thrombosis in a patient with protein S deficiency, and advises avoidance in people with thromboembolic history or elevated thrombotic risk and in women using combined hormonal contraception; it recommends a full history, informed consent about off-label use and stopping for visual symptoms or severe allergy.[6] Safety data for topical use come from the comparative trials above.[13][14]

The label states that published data have not clarified whether there is a drug-associated risk of miscarriage or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes, while Wikipedia says TXA appears safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding in its obstetric uses.[9][1]

As an antifibrinolytic, TXA occupies lysine-binding sites on plasminogen and plasmin, preventing binding to fibrin and preserving the clot matrix.[9] In skin, proposed actions include blocking the plasminogen activator pathway, reducing melanocyte activation from ultraviolet light, hormones and keratinocyte injury, lowering prostaglandin-related tyrosinase activity and reducing dermal angiogenesis.[6]

Tranexamic acid was first synthesized in 1962 by the Japanese researchers Shosuke and Utako Okamoto.[1] Its role in bleeding was established in large trials from 2010 onward, such as CRASH-2 in trauma (20,211 patients) and WOMAN in postpartum haemorrhage.[10][11] Its dermatological use for melasma developed later and remains off-label for the oral form.
The forum material reviewed contains almost no discussion of TXA for appearance; one T Nation poster mentions being prescribed it for bleeding.[18]

lore.intro: The forum sources reviewed contain very little about TXA, so community claims are sparse; the points below reflect how it is described in dermatology literature and skin-care discussion generally.

claims.claim: Oral tranexamic acid clears stubborn melasma
claims.believers: Some patients and practitioners describe it as a powerful option when topicals fail.[6]
claims.experts: A consensus and a systematic review report promising results but high relapse after stopping, unknown best duration and thrombosis-related screening needs.[3][6]

claims.claim: Topical TXA is as good as hydroquinone with fewer drawbacks
claims.believers: Skin-care users present it as a hydroquinone alternative.[13]
claims.experts: A split-face randomized trial compared 3 percent TXA with 4 percent hydroquinone in skin of color; reviews note hydroquinone remains the usual reference treatment.[13][3]

claims.claim: Tranexamic acid is just a cosmetic ingredient
claims.believers: Marketing of topical serums frames it as a brightening active.[4]
claims.experts: It is an antifibrinolytic prescription medicine with a thrombosis warning on its systemic labels; topical cosmetic concentrations have their own limited trials.[9][4]
